title: Celsus mocks our hope for the body
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς οὕτως λεγόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου πρὸς ἡμᾶς· ἔτι δὲ πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπα ὑμῶν ταῦτα, τὸ μὲν σῶμα ποθεῖν καὶ ἐλπίζειν ὅτι αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀναστήσεται ὡς οὐδὲν ἡμῖν τούτου κρεῖττον οὐδὲ τιμιώτερον, πάλιν δ᾿ αὐτὸ ῥίπτειν εἰς κολάσεις ὡς ἄτιμον; ἀλλὰ τοῖς μὲν τοῦτο πειθομένοις καὶ τῷ σώματι συντετηκόσιν οὐκ ἄξιον τοῦτο διαλέγεσθαι· οὗτοι γάρ εἰσιν οἱ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἄγροικοι καὶ ἀκάθαρτοι καὶ χωρὶς λόγου τῇ στάσει συννοσοῦντες· τοῖς μήν γε τὴν ψυχὴν ἢ τὸν νοῦν (εἴτε πνευματικὸν τοῦτον ἐθέλουσι καλεῖν εἴτε πνεῦμα νοερὸν ἅγιον καὶ μακάριον εἴτε ψυχὴν ζῶσαν εἴτε θείας καὶ ἀσωμάτου φύσεως ἔκγονον ὑπερουράνιόν τε καὶ ἄφθαρτον εἴθ᾿ ὅ τι καὶ ὅ τι χαίρουσιν ὀνομάζοντες), τοῖς τοῦτο ἐλπίζουσιν ἕξειν αἰώνιον σὺν θεῷ, τούτοις διαλέξομαι. τοῦτο μέν γε ὀρθῶς νομίζουσιν, ὡς οἱ μὲν εὖ βιώσαντες εὐδαιμονήσουσιν, οἱ δὲ ἄδικοι πάμπαν αἰωνίοις κακοῖς συνέξονται· καὶ τούτου δὲ τοῦ δόγματος μή θ᾿ οὗτοι μήτ᾿ ἄλλος ἀνθρώπων μηδείς ποτε ἀποστῇ † ἀποτείνοντες. περὶ ἀναστάσεως δὴ εἰ καὶ αὐτὸς ἤδη πολλάκις ὀνειδίζει, ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς τὸ κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἡμῖν φανὲν εὔλογον, (ὡς) οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν, παραστήσαντες οὐ μέλλομεν πρὸς ἓν ἔγκλημα πολλάκις λεγόμενον πολλάκις ἀπολογεῖσθαι. συκοφαντεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος ὡς οὐδὲν τοῦ σώματος κρεῖττον οὐδὲ τιμιώτερον ἐν τῇ συστάσει ἡμῶν ἡγουμένους· ψυχὴν γὰρ παντὸς σώματος καὶ μάλιστα τὴν λογικήν φαμεν εἶναι πρᾶγμα τιμιώτερον, εἰ καὶ τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος“ ψυχὴ μὲν χωρεῖ οὐδαμῶς δὲ τὸ σῶμα. οὐδὲ γὰρ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς σῶμα ὁ θεός· ἵνα μὴ περιπέσωμεν οἷς περιπίπτουσιν ἀτόποις οἱ τὰ Ζήνωνος καὶ Χρυσίππου φιλοσοφοῦντες.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see the next things said by Celsus to us: Further, how are not these of yours absurd (ἄτοπα), to long for (ποθεῖν) the body and hope (ἐλπίζειν) that this very thing will rise (ἀναστήσεται), as if nothing of ours were better (κρεῖττον) or more precious (τιμιώτερον) than it, and again to cast (ῥίπτειν) it into punishments as without honour (ἄτιμον)? But with those persuaded of this and melted together with (συντετηκόσιν) the body it is not worth discussing (διαλέγεσθαι) this; for these are those who also otherwise are boorish (ἄγροικοι) and unclean (ἀκάθαρτοι) and without reason (χωρὶς λόγου) share the sickness (συννοσοῦντες) of faction (στάσις); but with those who [hope] the soul or the mind (νοῦς) (whether they wish to call it spiritual (πνευματικόν), or intellectual spirit (πνεῦμα νοερόν) holy and blessed, or living soul (ψυχὴ ζῶσα), or offspring (ἔκγονον) of a divine and bodiless (ἀσωμάτου) nature, supercelestial (ὑπερουράνιον) and incorruptible (ἄφθαρτον), or whatever they rejoice to name it), with those who hope to have this eternal with God, with these I will discuss. This at least they rightly believe, that those who lived well will be happy (εὐδαιμονήσουσιν), and the unjust (ἄδικοι) will be held fast (συνέξονται) altogether (πάμπαν) by eternal evils; and from this doctrine (δόγμα) let neither these nor any other of men ever depart (ἀποστῇ) [† ἀποτείνοντες, corrupt]. — About resurrection, even if he himself already often reproaches (ὀνειδίζει), we, having set forth (παραστήσαντες) what appeared reasonable (εὔλογον) to us on the topic, as was possible, will not defend ourselves (ἀπολογεῖσθαι) many times against one charge (ἔγκλημα) said many times. Celsus slanders (συκοφαντεῖ) us as thinking nothing better or more precious than the body in our constitution (σύστασις); for we say the soul (ψυχή), and especially the rational (λογική), is a thing more precious than every body, since the soul admits (χωρεῖ) the 'according to the image of the one who created' (κατ' εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος), the body in no way. For not even in our view is God a body (σῶμα), so that we do not fall into the absurdities into which those philosophising Zeno's and Chrysippus's doctrines fall.
pass_b_english: Let us look also at what Celsus says to us next, which runs as follows: “And further, how is this not absurd of you, to long for the body and to hope that this very body will rise again, as though nothing in us were better or more precious than it, and then again to cast it into punishments as a thing without honour? But with those who are persuaded of this and are wedded to the body it is not worth reasoning about this matter; for these are people who are boorish and unclean in other respects too, and who, without reason, share in the sickness of faction. But those who hope that the soul or the mind (whether they wish to call it spiritual, or an intellectual spirit, holy and blessed, or a living soul (Genesis 2:7), or the incorruptible offspring, from beyond the heavens, of a divine and bodiless nature, or whatever name they like to give it) will be theirs for ever with God, with these I will reason. They are right at least in believing this: that those who have lived well will be happy, while the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils. And from this doctrine let neither these nor any other man ever depart.”

As to the resurrection, even if he himself has already reproached us with it many times, we have set forth, as best we could, what seemed reasonable to us on that subject, and we do not intend to make our defence many times over against one charge made many times over. But Celsus slanders us when he says that we think nothing in our make-up better or more precious than the body. For we say that the soul, and above all the rational soul, is a thing more precious than any body, since the soul can receive what is “according to the image of Him who created” it (Colossians 3:10), while the body cannot at all. For in our view God is not a body either, and so we do not fall into the absurdities into which those fall who follow the philosophy of Zeno and Chrysippus.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words run from ‘And further’ to ‘ever depart’. The text has an obelised corrupt word († ἀποτείνοντες) after ἀποστῇ; Origen repeats the sentence in 8.51 without it, so it is left untranslated here. τῇ στάσει συννοσοῦντες: Celsus elsewhere charges Christians with στάσις (faction, revolt against the common order); rendered ‘share in the sickness of faction’. Some editors suspect the text; sense kept literal. ‘Living soul’ (ψυχὴ ζῶσα) is Celsus using the Septuagint phrase of Genesis 2:7 (also quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:45); cited inline inside his quotation. ‘Spiritual’ may echo 1 Corinthians 15:44 but is not cited. τοῖς τοῦτο ἐλπίζουσιν ἕξειν αἰώνιον σὺν θεῷ: literally ‘who hope to have this [soul or mind] eternal with God’; rendered ‘will be theirs for ever with God’, which keeps the soul or mind as the thing held, as Origen’s paraphrase in 8.51 confirms. ἄτιμον rendered ‘without honour’ here and in 8.50, where Origen plays on τιμή, ἔντιμον and ἄτιμον. διαλέγεσθαι rendered ‘reason with’ throughout 8.49-8.50. κατ’ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος matches Colossians 3:10 (κατ’ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος αὐτόν), behind which stands Genesis 1:27; only Colossians cited inline. The Stoics (Zeno, Chrysippus) held God to be corporeal.
'will possess eternal life with God' -> 'will be theirs for ever with God' (ἕξειν αἰώνιον: the hopers will have the soul or mind eternal; 'life' was an addition and shifted the object)
'as worthless' -> 'as a thing without honour' (ἄτιμον; keeps the τιμή wordplay Origen answers in 8.50)
'discuss with' -> 'reason with' / 'reasoning about' (διαλέγεσθαι; natural English, consistent with 8.50)
'held fast altogether by eternal evils' -> 'held wholly in the grip of eternal evils' (πάμπαν ... συνέξονται; stiff order removed)
'is capable of being "according to the image..."' -> 'can receive what is "according to the image..."' (χωρεῖ); 'the body is not so at all' -> 'the body cannot at all' (οὐδαμῶς)
Genesis 2:7 (LXX εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν) and Colossians 3:10 (κατ' εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος) verified
